opus-5.5.text:
Well, the first thing to understand is that with O1, you don't even get to see the actual intermediate tokens. OpenAI hides them and gives you a summary, a sort of sanitized story about what supposedly happened. So right away there's a question: what is the relationship between what you're shown and what the model actually did to arrive at its answer? There's no particular reason to believe they're the same thing.

More broadly, I've been concerned for a while about anthropomorphizing these intermediate tokens. People look at chain-of-thought traces and say, "Oh look, it's thinking, it's reasoning just like we do." But these systems are trained, likely with some kind of reinforcement learning, to produce whatever token sequences lead to correct final answers. Nothing in that process forces the intermediate stuff to have any coherent semantics. In some of our own experiments, we've seen that you can train with traces that are noisy or even incorrect and still get improvements in final accuracy. So the traces work as a kind of prompt augmentation that helps the model get to an answer. They're not necessarily a faithful account of a reasoning process.

That's why the explanations worry me. If you take the summary as an explanation, you may be getting a post-hoc rationalization, something that sounds plausible to a human, rather than a causal account of how the answer was produced. And because it sounds so reasonable, people tend to trust it more. That's the dangerous part. You end up with false confidence. An explanation that reads well but doesn't correspond to the actual computation is arguably worse than no explanation at all, because it's actively misleading.

Humans do this too, of course. We often rationalize after the fact. But at least with humans we have a long history of calibrating how much to trust each other's explanations. With these systems, people's intuitions just haven't caught up.

So my position is this: judge these models on whether their final answers are correct, ideally checked by an external verifier, and be very careful about reading too much into the "reasoning" they show you. Whether a trace looks like reasoning and whether it actually is reasoning are two separate questions, and we shouldn't confuse them.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the explanation may be a post-hoc rationalization rather than a causal account of how the answer was produced, matching the criterion’s concern about explanations that do not consult the model’s actual route to its solution.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the first thing I'd say is that we should be careful with the word "explanation" here. What O1 produces are these intermediate tokens — OpenAI calls them reasoning tokens, and they show you a summary of them. People look at that and say, "Ah, this is the model's reasoning, it's showing me how it thinks." And my concern is that there is no guarantee whatsoever that those tokens are causally connected to the final answer in the way that a human explanation would be.

Think about what the system actually is. It's still an autoregressive model generating tokens. It generates a bunch of intermediate text, and then it generates the answer. Now, the intermediate text may well improve the accuracy of the answer — that is what the RL training is presumably optimizing for. But improving accuracy and faithfully describing the process are two very different things. The intermediate tokens are being selected because they lead to rewarded outcomes, not because they are true accounts of anything. So it's entirely possible for the model to produce a very plausible-looking derivation and then produce an answer that doesn't follow from it, or follows from something else entirely.

And in fact, OpenAI themselves more or less acknowledge this. They hide the raw chain of thought and say they're not training it to be presentable, and they're doing that partly because the raw thing can look incoherent or contradictory while still leading to a correct answer. That should tell you something. If the trace is doing its job as a sort of computational scratchpad — spending more tokens to effectively do more search — that doesn't make it an explanation. Explanation is a communication act. It has to be something that a human can verify, that actually tracks the reasons the conclusion holds.

So the danger is anthropomorphization. We see a text that looks like how we would talk through a problem, and we attribute to the system the kind of self-knowledge a person has when they explain themselves. But humans also confabulate — there's a whole psychology literature on post-hoc rationalization — and here we have a system that is, in a sense, trained to rationalize convincingly. People will trust the answer more because the explanation sounds good, and that is exactly backwards. If anything, you should be verifying these answers with external tools — a solver, a model checker, whatever is appropriate for the domain — rather than taking the generated trace as evidence of correctness. That's what I've been arguing with the LLM-Modulo approach: use the LLM for generation, but put the verification outside the model, where you can actually trust it.

r001.rationale: The response says O1’s intermediate text is not guaranteed to be causally connected to its answer and that the system may produce a plausible derivation that does not support the answer, describing it as trained to rationalize convincingly. This communicates the risk of an explanation becoming a post hoc defense.

astra-6.text:
What concerns me is that we tend to assume an explanation is a faithful account of how the system arrived at its answer. But those are two different things. A system can produce a very convincing explanation without that explanation being what actually caused it to give the answer.

With O1, we don’t have direct access to the internal reasoning process. So when it gives us an account of its reasoning, how do we know whether that account reflects the computation or is a plausible story constructed afterward? The explanation alone cannot establish that.

That doesn’t mean the system can’t solve problems. It means we should distinguish its ability to get an answer, its ability to justify that answer, and our ability to understand how it got there. A justification can be checked independently and still tell us very little about the underlying process. My worry is that fluent explanations encourage us to collapse those distinctions and attribute more transparency to the system than we actually have.

r001.rationale: The response says an explanation may be a plausible story constructed afterward rather than reflect the computation that produced the answer, capturing a post hoc defense that does not consult the model’s actual reasoning.

sol-6.1.text:
My concern is that we’re conflating an explanation of reasoning with the reasoning itself. When O1 gives you a plausible account of how it arrived at an answer, what establishes that this account faithfully reflects the process that produced the answer? It could be a post hoc rationalization.

That doesn’t mean the answer is necessarily wrong, or that the explanation is useless. But you can’t take the explanation as independent evidence that the system reasoned correctly. If you want that assurance, you need some way to check the steps and the conclusion independently. A convincing story about why an answer is right is not the same as a verification that it is right.

r001.rationale: The response questions whether an explanation faithfully reflects the process that produced the answer and says it could be a post hoc rationalization, capturing the risk of an explanation serving as a defense without consulting the actual reasoning.
